subject: Climate & Environment
title: Cooking with Solid Fuels
description: A 60-second lesson on Cooking with Solid Fuels.

hook.text: About 2.4 billion people cook over open fires fueled by wood, dung, or charcoal.

buildup.text: Smoke fills kitchens with PM2.5 levels 20 times higher than a polluted city street.

discovery.text: Household air pollution kills about 3.2 million people each year — mostly women and children.

twist.text: Clean cookstoves exist and cost as little as $25. Distribution is the real barrier.

climax.text: Switching to LPG or electric stoves slashes indoor pollution by over 90% immediately.

punchline.text: The deadliest air pollution isn't outside. It's in the kitchen.

quiz.question: How many people still cook over open fires with solid fuels?

details.summary: Nearly three billion people cook with wood, charcoal, coal, or dung, producing thick indoor smoke laden with PM2.5 and carbon monoxide. Household air pollution from solid fuels kills an estimated 3.2 million people annually, mostly women and children.
details.whyItMatters: Household air pollution is a top-five global health risk. Clean cookstove programs address poverty, gender inequality, deforestation, and climate change simultaneously.
takeaways: Solid fuel smoke contains PM2.5, CO, and carcinogenic compounds
Women and children suffer most due to time spent near the hearth
LPG and electric stoves dramatically reduce indoor exposure

faq.question: Why do billions of people still cook with solid fuels?
faq.answer: Wood, dung, and charcoal are freely available or cheap in rural areas where gas and electricity infrastructure is absent or unaffordable. Cultural preferences and supply chains also sustain traditional fuel use.

faq.question: How much do clean cookstoves reduce indoor pollution?
faq.answer: LPG stoves reduce kitchen PM2.5 by 80 to 90 percent compared to open fires. Improved biomass stoves with chimneys cut exposure by 30 to 60 percent but still fall short of WHO guidelines.
